\chapter{The Wardrobe, And The Word For Having No Work}
\label{ch:paro-y-ropa}
\hlchaptermodality{430}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that somebody is out of work, read a clothes-shop price list, and name the three garments the corpus was missing.}

Read a sale board with three garments and three prices, say which is cheapest and what you would buy, and answer whether you are working.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[estar en paro]{estar en paro — the halt, rather than the missing job}

\label{lesson:ES-C430-estar-en-paro}



\begin{quote}
You can say \emph{el trabajo}. Try to say that somebody has none, and notice English reaches for a word built on \emph{employ} that Spanish does not use in conversation.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: estar en paro}
\textbf{estar en paro} — to be unemployed, to be out of work.

\emph{Mi hermano está en paro.} — \textquotedblleft{}My brother is out of work.\textquotedblright{}

\textbf{El paro} on its own is both the state and the benefit paid during it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{El paro} is built straight off \textbf{parar}, \textquotedblleft{}to stop\textquotedblright{} — so it is a \textbf{stoppage}. Spanish names the situation after \textbf{the halt}, where English names it after the missing employment.

The verb has a startling history. Latin \textbf{parare} meant \textbf{to make ready} — the root inside \emph{preparar} and \emph{reparar}. The sense travelled in steps: \emph{to get ready} became \emph{to stand ready}, and \emph{to stand ready} became \textbf{to stand still}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{where on the journey} \\
\midrule
pre\textbf{para}r & to make ready beforehand \\
\textbf{para}r & to stand still \\
el \textbf{paro} & the standing still itself \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{estar en paro} is, underneath, \textbf{being in the halt}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: which verb, and which country}]
It takes \textbf{estar} rather than \textbf{ser}, because it names a situation rather than a person, and situations change.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{where} & \textbf{the everyday word} \\
\midrule
Spain & el paro \\
much of Latin America & el desempleo \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Desempleo} is the formal word everywhere, and the one a newspaper prints. A person in Spain talking about their own life says \textbf{paro}.

The pair a form will ask you to choose between is short: \emph{tengo trabajo} against \emph{estoy en paro}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}estar en paro\textquotedblright{} — to be out of work
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Mi hermano está en paro\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two halves of the pair — having work, and being in the halt
  \item what \emph{parare} meant in Latin, and the two steps to \emph{stop}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb does \emph{en paro} take, \emph{ser} or \emph{estar}? (\textbf{Estar} — it is a situation.) What does \emph{el paro} literally name? (The stoppage.) Which word would a newspaper print instead? (\emph{El desempleo}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[los vaqueros]{los vaqueros — trousers named after the man who wore them}

\label{lesson:ES-C430-vaqueros}



\begin{quote}
You can say \emph{el pantalón} for trousers in general. Name the one kind of trousers almost everybody in the room is wearing, and see whether you have a word for it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: los vaqueros}
\textbf{los vaqueros} — jeans.

Always plural, the way \emph{pantalones} is, because the garment has two legs.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{La vaca} is a cow, from Latin \textbf{vacca}. A \textbf{vaquero} is the man who looks after them — a cowherd, and in the Americas a \textbf{cowboy}.

Jeans arrived in Spain as the trousers those men wore, and Spanish named them after \textbf{the wearer} rather than the cloth. English went the other way: \emph{jeans} comes from \textbf{Genoa}, the Italian port whose hard cotton the trousers were cut from, and \emph{denim} from \emph{de Nîmes}, the French town. Three languages, three different things noticed about the same garment.

Some regions say \textbf{los tejanos} instead — \textquotedblleft{}the Texans\textquotedblright{} — which is the same thought arriving from a different direction.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: garments that come in pairs}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{garment} & \textbf{usual number} \\
\midrule
los vaqueros & plural \\
los pantalones & plural \\
la camisa & singular \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Anything with two legs tends to arrive plural. Spanish tolerates \emph{el pantalón} in the singular, and does \textbf{not} do the same for \emph{vaqueros} — you will hear the plural every time.

The \textbf{v} and the \textbf{b} sound alike in Spanish, so \emph{vaquero} opens with the same soft sound as \emph{bueno}. Spelling keeps the Latin \textbf{v}; the mouth stopped distinguishing them centuries ago.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}los vaqueros\textquotedblright{} — jeans
  \item what a \emph{vaquero} is when it is a person
  \item which garments Spanish keeps plural, and why
  \item where English \emph{jeans} and \emph{denim} come from
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What animal is hiding in \emph{vaqueros}? (\emph{La vaca}, the cow.) What did English name the same trousers after? (Two cities — Genoa and Nîmes.) Would you say \emph{el vaquero} for the garment? (No — the garment is plural.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el jersey]{el jersey — an island, worn}

\label{lesson:ES-C430-jersey}



\begin{quote}
You can say \emph{la camisa}. Name what you put \textbf{over} it when the weather turns, and see whether the word is there.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el jersey}
\textbf{el jersey} — the jumper, the pullover, the sweater.

Said the Spanish way: \emph{jer-SÉI}, with the \textbf{j} as the throaty \emph{jota} you already have from \emph{jamón}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Jersey} is an island in the Channel, between England and France. Its knitters were famous, and the heavy woollen garment they made took the island's name in English. Spanish borrowed the English word entire, island and all.

That makes it one of a small set of Spanish clothing words that name a \textbf{place} rather than a shape or a material:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{garment} & \textbf{the place} \\
\midrule
el jersey & a Channel island \\
los tejanos & Texas \\
la chaqueta & a French peasant named Jacques \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Latin America mostly says \textbf{el suéter} instead — also English, borrowed a different way, and spelled to fit Spanish.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what a borrowed word has to learn}]
A word taken from another language still has to obey the accent rules of this one. \emph{Jersey} is stressed on its last syllable, and a word ending in \textbf{-y} takes no written accent, so the singular is bare.

The plural is where it shows:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{number} & \textbf{form} \\
\midrule
singular & el jersey \\
plural & los jerséis \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The \textbf{y} turns into an \textbf{i}, the ending becomes \textbf{-s}, and now an accent is needed to hold the stress where it was. Spanish did not leave the word foreign; it made it follow the rules.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el jersey\textquotedblright{} — \emph{jer-SÉI}
  \item the plural, and hear where the accent has to appear
  \item what Jersey is, before it was a garment
  \item the word much of Latin America uses instead
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is a \emph{jersey}, before it is clothing? (An island in the Channel.) What is the plural? (\emph{Los jerséis} — with a written accent.) Why does the accent appear only in the plural? (The ending changes, so the stress needs holding.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el bolso]{el bolso — a hide, a purse, and one vowel that changes the object}

\label{lesson:ES-C430-bolso}



\begin{quote}
You have clothes and now a jumper. Name the thing carried \textbf{beside} the clothes rather than worn, and see whether you have it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el bolso}
\textbf{el bolso} — the handbag.

Not a shopping bag and not a pocket. A \emph{bolso} is the bag carried on the arm or shoulder, and a shop will file it under accessories beside the shoes.

\begin{cousinweb}
Greek \textbf{byrsa} meant \textbf{a hide, a piece of worked leather}. Latin took it as \textbf{bursa}, and because a leather pouch is what money was carried in, the word came to mean \textbf{purse}.

From that one pouch:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{what it kept} \\
\midrule
el bolso & the bag on your arm \\
el bolsillo & the little one sewn into your clothes \\
la bolsa & the bag, and the stock exchange \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English got \textbf{bursar}, \textbf{reimburse} and \textbf{purse} from the same leather.

The stock-exchange sense is the strangest and the best attested: traders in fifteenth-century Bruges met at the house of a family called \textbf{Van der Buerse}, and the name of the meeting place became the name of the market everywhere.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the vowel that picks the object}]
\textbf{Bolso} and \textbf{bolsa} are one letter apart and name different things:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{what it is} \\
\midrule
el bolso & a handbag \\
la bolsa & a bag, a carrier bag, the stock exchange \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Ask for \emph{una bolsa} in a shop and you get something to carry the shopping home in. Ask for \emph{un bolso} and you are shown the leather goods.

This is a pattern worth knowing rather than a single oddity: Spanish sometimes uses the \textbf{-o / -a} pair to separate two related objects rather than two genders of one. You have already met \emph{el pantalón} keeping its own shape for the same kind of reason.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el bolso\textquotedblright{} — the handbag
  \item what \emph{una bolsa} would get you in a shop instead
  \item what \emph{byrsa} meant, and what it was used to carry
  \item the word for the small one sewn into your clothes
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of \emph{bolso} and \emph{bolsa} is the handbag? (\emph{El bolso}.) What did the Greek word name? (A hide.) What else does \emph{la bolsa} mean? (The stock exchange — after a family's house in Bruges.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cuatro que cierran dos listas]{cuatro que cierran dos listas — four words, two finished lists}

\label{lesson:ES-C430-repaso-piezas}



\begin{quote}
Say the two halves of the work pair — having it, and not having it — before you read on.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the wardrobe, complete}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{garment} & \textbf{already yours} \\
\midrule
el pantalón & yes \\
la falda & yes \\
la camisa & yes \\
el zapato & yes \\
los vaqueros & new \\
el jersey & new \\
el bolso & new \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Four were taught across earlier chapters and three arrived here. The list an exam works from is now covered end to end, which is what the three were for.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: each one's own trap}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{what to watch} \\
\midrule
estar en paro & takes \emph{estar}, and \emph{paro} means the halt \\
los vaqueros & plural every time \\
el jersey & plural \emph{jerséis}, with a written accent \\
el bolso & \emph{la bolsa} is a different object \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: where each word came from}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{named after} \\
\midrule
el paro & the stopping \\
los vaqueros & the cowherd \\
el jersey & an island \\
el bolso & a leather hide \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three of the four are named after something other than themselves — a person, a place, a material. That is a habit worth noticing, because it is how a reader guesses at a word they have not met.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the seven garments, running through the whole wardrobe
  \item the plural of \emph{jersey}
  \item the difference between \emph{el bolso} and \emph{la bolsa}
  \item which verb goes with \emph{en paro}, and why
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which garment is always plural? (\emph{Los vaqueros}.) Which word changes object when you change its last vowel? (\emph{Bolso} against \emph{bolsa}.) What does \emph{el paro} name? (The halt.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Synthesis — a shop window and a sentence about yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C430-sintesis-anuncio}



\begin{quote}
Name the three garments this chapter added, before they appear in a price list.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{ROPA — REBAJAS}
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{artículo} & \textbf{precio} \\
\midrule
vaqueros & 25 € \\
jerséis & 18 € \\
bolsos & 30 € \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every line is readable, and one of them is teaching you something: the middle row is a \textbf{plural}, and the accent on \emph{jerséis} is exactly where the singular did not need one.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection*{How to answer}
Say what is cheapest, what is dearest, and what you would buy:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Los jerséis son los más baratos.} \emph{Quiero unos vaqueros.}
\end{quote}

Note \emph{unos vaqueros} rather than \emph{un vaquero}. A pair of trousers is a plural thing, so the article is plural too.

\subsection*{The exchange}
The other half of the chapter, in the two lines a form or an interview wants:

\begin{quote}
— \emph{¿Trabajas?} — \emph{No, estoy en paro.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Estoy}, not \emph{soy}. Being out of work is a situation, and Spanish keeps situations away from \emph{ser}. The same answer in the positive is \emph{sí, tengo trabajo} — the noun you have had since the professions chapter, finally with a negative to stand against.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three prices with their garments
  \item which row carries a written accent, and where the singular has none
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Quiero unos vaqueros\textquotedblright{}, and say why the article is plural
  \item both answers to \emph{¿Trabajas?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb answers \emph{¿Trabajas?} in the negative? (\emph{Estoy} — \emph{estoy en paro}.) Which word in the price list gained an accent in the plural? (\emph{Jerséis}.) Why \emph{unos vaqueros} rather than \emph{un}? (The garment is plural.)
\end{tcolorbox}
